title: Demons, Passions, and Dreams
english: Having suddenly entered there, they seize the struggling soul. The evil demons draw their even more evil demons to their aid; and while opposing one another according to their dispositions, they agree only upon the destruction of the soul.

But let not the demon who snatches away the mind toward blasphemy against God and toward those unmentionable fantasies which I have not dared to hand over even by writing trouble us, nor let him cut off our readiness; for the Lord is a searcher of hearts and knows that, even while being in the world, we never raved with such madness. The aim of this demon is to make us cease from prayer, so that we may not stand before the Lord our God, nor dare to stretch out our hands, against whom we have thought such things.

For the passions in the soul are signaled either by some word brought forward beforehand, or by a movement of the body occurring, through which the enemies perceive whether we have their thoughts within us and are in travail, or whether, having rejected them, we are anxious for our salvation. For God who made us alone knows the mind, and he himself does not need signals to know the things hidden in the heart.

For those in the world, the demons wrestle more through external things, but for the monks, mostly through thoughts; for through external things they are lacking because of the desert. And as it is easier to sin by thought than by deed, so much more difficult is the war by thought than that composed of external things; for the mind is a movable thing and difficult to settle against lawless fantasies.

We have not been commanded to work continually and to keep watch and to fast, but it has been legislated for us to pray unceasingly; for those heal the passive part of the soul but need our body for the work, which through its own weakness is not sufficient for the labors; but prayer strengthens the mind and prepares it pure for the struggle, being by nature fitted to pray even apart from this body, and to fight the demons on behalf of all the powers of the soul. If any of the monks would wish to make trial of wild demons and to get a habit of their craft, let him guard his thoughts, and let him mark their intensifications, and the...

Seek from Christ the words concerning these things: the movements, the transmigrations, the times, which demons are doing these things, and which demon a person follows, and who follows whom. For they rage greatly at those pursuing the practical life more knowingly, wishing to shoot down in the moonless night those upright in heart.

You will find two very sharp demons almost running ahead of the movement of our mind: the demon of fornication and the one seizing us toward blasphemy against God; but the latter is short-lived, while the former, unless it moves the thoughts with passion, will not hinder us from the knowledge of God.

To separate body from soul belongs only to him who bound them together; but to separate soul from body belongs also to the one who longs for virtue. For our Fathers name withdrawal the practice of death and flight from the body.

Those who nourish the flesh badly and make provision for it unto desires, let them blame it; for those who have acquired the soul's dispassion through this body and apply it to the contemplation of beings know the grace of the Creator.

Regarding what happens in dreams: When the demons, fighting in the dream-phantasies against the desiring part, themselves show — but we run toward — gatherings of acquaintances and banquets of relatives and dances of women, and all other such things productive of pleasures, in this part we are sick and the passion is strong. When they again disturb the irascible part, forcing us to walk on precipitous paths, bringing armed men and venomous and flesh-eating beasts, while we are terrified by the paths and flee, pursued by the beasts and men, let us make provision for the irascible part, and calling upon Christ in vigils, let us use the aforementioned remedies.

The imageless natural movements of the body in sleep indicate to some extent that the soul is healthy; but fixation of images is a sign of sickness; and consider the indefinite faces a sign of the old passion, and the defined ones a symbol of the fresh wound.
The proofs of dispassion are, by day, through the thoughts, and by night...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Signs of Apatheia and Practical Insights
english: Through dreams we come to know these things. And we say that dispassion is health for the soul, and knowledge its nourishment, which alone is accustomed to join us to the holy powers, if indeed union with the incorporeal naturally comes about from a similar disposition.

There are two peaceful states of the soul: one rising from the natural seeds, the other supervening from the withdrawal of the demons. Upon the former follow humility with compunction, and a tear and an infinite longing toward the Divine, and an immeasurable zeal for the work; upon the latter, vainglory with pride, drawing the monk down through the destruction of the other demons. Therefore, he who keeps the boundaries of the former state will more keenly recognize the attacks of the demons.

The demon of vainglory opposes the demon of fornication, and for these to attack a soul together is among impossibilities; if indeed the one promises honors, the other becomes a procurer of dishonors. Whichever of these, then, having approached, presses you, fashion, supposedly, within yourself the thoughts of the opposing demon; and if you can drive out, as the saying goes, nail with nail, know that you are near the boundaries of dispassion; for your mind has been strong enough to annihilate the thoughts of demons with human thoughts. But to repel the thought of vainglory through humility, or the thought of fornication through sobriety, would be the deepest evidence of dispassion. And try to do this against all the demons opposed to one another; for at the same time you will also know by which passion you have been more qualified. But as much as possible, ask from God to defend against the enemies in the second way.

As much as the soul advances, so much greater adversaries succeed it; for I am not persuaded that the same demons always remain with it; and this is known most by those who apply themselves more keenly to temptations, and see their present dispassion being pried out by the successors. Perfect dispassion comes to the soul after the victory over all the adversaries in the practical struggle against the demons; but imperfect dispassion is so called with respect to the power, for now, of the demon wrestling with it.

The mind would not advance, nor would it journey that beautiful journey, and come to be in the land of the incorporeal, without having set its inner things right; for the disturbance of its own things tends to turn it back toward those from which it had departed.
Both virtues and vices make the mind blind: the former, so that it may not see vices; the latter, so that it may not again see virtues.

Regarding the signs of dispassion: When the mind begins to perform the prayers without distraction, then the whole war is established regarding the irascible part of the soul, both at night and by day.
A sign of dispassion is a mind beginning to see its own light, remaining quiet toward the phantasms of sleep, and beholding realities smoothly.
The mind is strong imagining nothing of this world during the time of prayer.

A mind having accomplished the practical with God and approached knowledge perceives little or not at all the irrational part of the soul, knowledge seizing it aloft and separating it from sensible things.
A soul has dispassion, not one that does not suffer with respect to things, but one that remains undisturbed even with respect to their memories.
The perfect does not practice self-control, and the dispassionate does not endure, if endurance belongs to the one suffering, and self-control to the one being tossed about.
Great indeed is to pray without distraction, but greater is to also sing without distraction.
He who has established the virtues within himself, and having been wholly mixed with these, no longer remembers law or commandments or punishment, but says and does whatever the best state dictates.

Practical insights: The demonic songs move our desire, and cast shameful phantasies into the soul; but the psalms and hymns and the spiritual songs always call the mind to the memory of virtue, cooling our boiling thumos and withering the desires.

If wrestlers consist in pressing and counter-pressing, and the demons wrestle with us, then they themselves, pressing us, are counter-pressed by us. For I shall press them out, he says, and they will not be able to stand. And again: those pressing me and my enemies themselves grew weak and fell.
Rest is joined with wisdom, and toil with prudence; for there is not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Tripartite Soul and its Virtues
english: To acquire wisdom without war is impossible, and one cannot win the war without prudence; for this is entrusted to resist the thumos of the demons, forcing the powers of the soul to act according to nature and making the way of wisdom easy. 74 A temptation is a monk's thought ascending through the passive part of the soul and darkening the mind. 75 Sin is a monk's assent of the thought toward a forbidden pleasure. 76 Angels rejoice when evil is diminished, but demons when virtue is; for the former are servants of mercy and love, while the latter are obedient to anger and hatred; and the former, approaching, fill us with spiritual theoria, while the latter, approaching, cast shameful fantasies into the soul. 77 Virtues do not stop the impulses of the demons, but they preserve us innocent. 78 Practical method is a spiritual method cleansing the passive part of the soul. 79 The workings of the commandments are not sufficient to perfectly heal the powers of the soul, unless fitting theoriai also succeed the mind. 80 It is not possible for us to resist all the thoughts cast at us by angels, but it is possible to overthrow all the thoughts from demons; for a peaceful state follows the former thoughts, but a disturbed one the latter. 81 Love is the offspring of dispassion; and dispassion is the flower of practice; and practice is established by the keeping of the commandments; and the guardian of these is the fear of God, which is the offspring of right faith; and faith is an inward good, which is naturally present even in those who do not yet believe in God. 82 Just as the soul acting through the body perceives the weak members, so the mind, acting, knows its own proper energy and its own powers, and through what obstructs it discovers the soul's therapeutic commandment. 83 The mind, waging the passionate war, will not behold the logoi of the war; for it is like one fighting in the night; but having acquired dispassion, it will easily recognize the methods of the enemies. 84 The end of practice is love; the end of knowledge is theology; the beginnings of both are faith and natural theoria; and as many as
The text ends abruptly with 'and as many as' (καὶ ὅσοι).

On the one hand, as many demons as touch the passive part of the soul are said to oppose practice; but as many as disturb the rational part are named enemies of all truth and contrary to theoria. None of the things that defile bodies associates thereafter with the purified; but the virtues both purify the soul and remain with the purified.

By nature, the rational soul acts when its desiring part reaches for virtue, its spirited part struggles on its behalf, and its rational part applies itself to the theoria of things that have come to be. He who progresses in practice diminishes the passions, while he in theoria diminishes ignorance; for of the passions there shall one day be a total destruction, but of ignorance, of the one they say there is an end, of the other that there is not.

The goods and evils beyond use become productive of virtues and vices; it belongs to prudence to use these toward other ends. Since the rational soul is threefold according to our wise teacher, when virtue comes to be in the rational part, it is called prudence, understanding, and wisdom; when in the desiring part, temperance, love, and self-control; when in the irascible part, courage and endurance; but in the whole soul, justice. And the work of prudence is to strategize against the opposing powers, to defend the virtues, to array oneself against the vices, and to manage the intermediate things according to the seasons; of understanding, to harmoniously manage all things contributing to us toward the goal; of wisdom, to behold the logoi of bodily and incorporeal things; of temperance, the work is to look dispassionately at the things that move irrational imaginations within us; of love, to present itself to every image of God as nearly like the prototype, even if the demons attempt to defile them; of self-control, to shake off all pleasure of the throat with joy; not to fear enemies and to bravely withstand the terrible belongs to endurance and courage; of justice, to produce a certain concord and harmony of the parts of the soul.
Sheaves are the fruit of seeds, and knowledge of virtues; and as tears follow seeds, so joy follows sheaves.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
